extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history (readers of H. G. Wells / popular world history)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository historical account of how education, religion, printing, and social upheaval (Black Death, peasant revolts, Reformation) shaped mass opinion, government, and social change in medieval and early modern Europe. The text argues causal and normative principles about information, education, and political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of knowledge limits community of will
rubrics_metrics.description: The community of will is limited in size by the limitations set upon the possibilities of a community of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A medium of general information and wide organization of education are necessary to make citizens 'willing' to act collectively; the concentration of property and replacement of free workers by slaves were made possible by decay of public spirit and confusion of public intelligence resulting from limited shared knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information must precede consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Information must precede consultation; the modern citizen must be informed first and then consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before he can vote he must hear the evidence; before he can decide he must know. Votes by uneducated people are useless and dangerous. The pathway from servitude to cooperative modern state is set up by schools and universal access to literature, knowledge, and news rather than by merely setting up polling booths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational government as modern ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern ideal of government is an educational government in which the ordinary man is informed, inspired, and consulted rather than ruled by an absolute monarch or demagogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is a collective function not a private affair; creating courts of consultation without prior education fails. The state's role includes providing universal education and accessible information to create a community of knowledge and will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written word/propaganda links masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained propagandas and the power of the written word can link great multitudes of diverse men in common enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both Christianity and Islam relied successfully on written texts to supply common moral education, common history, and a common idea of human purpose; organized propagandas can impose a unifying idea across unprecedented areas and populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological prerequisites for mass dissemination (paper + printing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheap and abundant paper manufacture and movable-type printing are prerequisites for the wide multiplication of books and the spread of literacy and free discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper originated in China and its manufacture reached Christian Europe by the 13th–14th centuries (Italy then Germany); only when paper was abundant and cheap did printing become a practicable business and make the intellectual life of the world enter a vigorous phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainer books enable independent thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed books that are plainer and easier to read allow readers to think as they read rather than merely copy or decipher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift from decorated manuscripts to plainly printed texts expanded the reading public, encouraged authors to write for ordinary readers, and fostered development and standardization of national literary languages capable of philosophical discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common moral education and shared historical narrative unify populations
rubrics_metrics.description: To hold large and diverse populations together requires a common moral education and a common history of the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christianity and Islam supplied, in their distinctive ways, this gap that republican systems couldn't fill, creating a shallow but effective community of will over unprecedented areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Reformation motives (princes / people / within-church)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reformation took three distinct forms: the princes' Reformation (political, to seize church resources and authority), the people's Reformation (religious, to secure a righteous and effective church), and the Reformation within the church (internal moral/organizational renewal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three aspects often intermingled and produced different outcomes; evaluating a given reform requires assessing which of the three motives predominated and how each actor sought to control or direct change.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-controlled reform requires limiting popular radicalism
rubrics_metrics.description: When rulers (princes) adopt reform, they typically aim to use popular forces against the Pope while keeping those forces subordinate to state power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful princely reformation allows 'just as much reformation as would sever the link with Rome' but resists dangerous breaks toward primitive or radical interpretations; the Established Church of England exemplifies a compromise that preserved state control while adopting some reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theological doctrines structure institutional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal positions (e.g., transubstantiation vs. memorialism about the mass) directly affect the necessity and authority of the priesthood within Christian institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief that the sacrament requires a priest to effect a miraculous change increases priestly power; the view that the sacrament is a personal remembrance reduces the institutional need for consecrated priests and undermines clerical dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass availability of sacred texts fosters diverse interpretation and Nonconformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The printed and translated Bible set up a counter-authority to the church and produced a wide variety of individual readings, interpretations, and sects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility of scripture encouraged ‘strange and grotesque’ interpretations but also empowered lay conscience; this literacy-driven pluralism produced Nonconformists and a persistent residuum resistant to imposed ecclesiastical control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic mismanagement in crises provokes popular revolt
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh or ignorant economic policies by elites in times of crisis (e.g., laws compelling labor without wage increases after the Black Death) provoke social unrest and uprisings among the labouring classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the Black Death, scarcity of labor and rigid statutes designed to suppress wages and movement prompted peasant wars (English revolt, Jacquerie, Hussite disturbances, later German Peasant Wars); failure to adjust economic arrangements in crisis undermines social stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious movements inadvertently spread egalitarian ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious teachings and missionary activity can unintentionally propagate ideas of equality, freedom, and human dignity among common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when institutional religion did not intend to promote equalitarian doctrines, the personality and teachings of figures like Jesus carried seeds of freedom and responsibility that later informed labour movements and egalitarian impulses in modern civilizations.
